questions.q: Which circuit builds a 3-qubit GHZ state?
questions.explain: The GHZ state is built by putting one qubit into superposition with H, then chaining CX gates (cx(0,1), then cx(1,2)) to propagate that superposition out across all three qubits.

questions.q: What are the exact ideal probabilities for the 3-qubit GHZ state?
options: P(000)=0.25, P(111)=0.25, remaining probability split across the other 6 outcomes
P(000)=0.5, P(111)=0.5, all 6 other outcomes exactly 0
Equal 1/8 probability on all 8 outcomes
P(000)=1.0, all other outcomes 0
questions.explain: The GHZ state (|000>+|111>)/sqrt(2) has amplitude 0.7071068 only on |000> and |111>, giving exact probability 0.5 to each and exactly zero to the other six 3-bit combinations.

questions.q: A real 2048-shot run of the GHZ circuit gave {'000': 1069, '111': 979} with the other 6 outcomes at exactly 0. What does the 1069-vs-979 gap represent?
options: A structural zero, like the other six outcomes
Ordinary statistical shot noise around the true 50/50 ideal split
Evidence the circuit was built incorrectly
Proof that the qubits were not entangled
questions.explain: Even with an exact 0.5/0.5 ideal split, a finite number of shots will rarely land on a perfect even count. This gap is expected statistical variation, the same phenomenon seen in the chapter's earlier single- and two-qubit examples.

questions.q: A classmate's run of the same GHZ circuit shows {'000': 1041, '111': 1003, '101': 4}. What should this nonzero '101' count prompt them to check first?
options: Whether they used too many shots
Nothing — it's within normal shot noise, just like the 000/111 split
Whether their circuit has a bug (e.g. wrong qubit order or gate) or whether real hardware noise is present, since '101' is a structural zero that should never appear from shot noise alone
Whether they forgot to call qc.draw()
questions.explain: Unlike the 000/111 split, '101' has exactly zero amplitude in the ideal GHZ state. A nonzero count there is not explainable by ordinary shot noise and points to either a circuit construction error or real noise effects (covered in Chapter 7), not something to ignore.

questions.q: Why is 'predict the outcome distribution before running the circuit' presented as a core skill in this lab, rather than just a teaching exercise?
options: Because Qiskit requires a prediction to be submitted before running any circuit
Because it builds the habit of treating a mismatch between prediction and real results as a signal worth investigating, which scales to circuits too large to trace by hand
Because shots cost money and predicting avoids running the circuit at all
Because simulators are unreliable and predictions are usually more accurate
questions.explain: The practical value is catching mistakes: once circuits get too complex to mentally trace, comparing a stated prediction against the real run is the main way to notice something went wrong.
